utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But regardless of this explanation, I imagine that you are not questioning the fact that they were present and that journalists were present, as a matter of fact, during the police operation.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were clearly OSCE people up on the ridge, and it was those people whose report came to me, saying that there was a major operation going on in this area, which caused me to send Maisonneuve down there so that he could bring his experienced eye to bear on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means that from the beginning of the operation they were there, but they were not experienced enough, but then Maisonneuve came because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That is not what the witness said. But let's move on. We've exhausted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you did not see any evidence of any kind of fighting there. As a matter of fact, you made the assertion that the KLA had left the area, that is to say that there had not been any fighting. That is what you claimed.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my impression, yes, and I can certainly confirm that the area that I walked over, which was the trench system behind the village, had not been fought over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Allow me to remind you yet again, in view of the position and in view of what you had heard and in view of what you had seen from your Verification Mission, and it seems to me that you had to know this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please play the second video clip. Could we please hear the soundtrack as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this relates to what you said, that there had been no fighting and that you had not seen anything on the basis of which one could conclude that there had been fighting in Racak. I'm not going to play the entire film. I'm keeping it for yet another witness. My question is the following: Is it truly possible that you did not know a thing about this? You have two vehicles that are following the action, there are a few foreign TV crews and groups of journalists there and you did not know a thing about this; is that really possible?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was up at Pec. I was not in Pristina where the communications normally went back to. And the report came to me via Pristina, so it took a bit longer. There had been instances when the first report was not exactly what really happened, which was why I wanted someone with a lot of experience to go there and find out what really was happening. I certainly didn't have the benefit of any film at the time. I would add that the film clip that I've just seen shows that there were -- and I heard the fighting -- the firing, shows that heavy weapons were being used, which were only owned by your forces, to support the entry into the village. There was then small-arms fire, which could have come from anybody, but in my experience, your police tended to fire at areas that might contain something they were worried about. They certainly didn't wait until they saw a target before they opened fire. So everything I've seen on that film clip shows that your police went into the village supported by heavy fire, probably firing at anything that moved or look suspicious. I didn't see any evidence on there of fighting coming back -- firing coming back in the opposite direction. So it is possible that the KLA were there at the start of the operation. It's also quite possible that they ran away quite quickly, as they often did, and that your people went into a village from which the KLA had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that they fired regardless of the fact that there were no KLA people there.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That often happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, does it seem to be logical to you, General, that the police should call the journalists, the cameramen, inform the OSCE and observers and monitors to attend and follow some sort of massacre?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you informed the whole of the world public that this was indeed a massacre and that civilians had been killed. This triggered off a reaction on the part of many statesmen. Now, you made your assessment although you had not completed an investigation or conducted post-mortems and things of that kind; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had not conducted post-mortems. The judgement was made on the basis of the facts as they were seen at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you so quick then? Why were you in a hurry?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we were in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Racak was a pretext for the bombing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a proper question. You can ask the witness about what he saw or heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right, then. Did you hear or see that Walker, on the 10th of April, 2000, in Bonn, made the statement to the effect that the episode in Racak was decisive for the bombing; and do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, answer me this: Why did you not -- or, for example, perhaps you didn't want to look at some facts. And during your stay in Kosovo, were you aware of the facts and figures by the committee that conducted the post-mortems? I'm going to read out just some of the points. And the document is one which was disclosed by the Prosecutor, which includes part of that report. It is the Association of Physicians that I'm going to quote, from KO212750. That is the number of the document. It is page 73, and just the conclusion made by the professors who conducted the post-mortems and provided evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask Mr. May something? Could you clarify for me, please, whether the time, if I am presenting documents, be deducted from my overall cross-examination time or not? Your answer is very important to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be added?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It will be part of the whole.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it can only be within the space of two hours, is that it, altogether?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then I won't place the documents on the ELMO, on the overhead projector - it takes too much time - but I shall be giving them to you. They are the documents that I received with the numbers I received. And it says: "With all 40 post-mortems that were carried out there was not a single detail in which the opinions of all experts present were not of accord." Then it says: "The presence of nitrate was found in 37 of the 40 bodies that were examined in the post-mortem. Throughout our work in the post-mortem halls, we had the presence of other people, the second secretary of the Finnish embassy in Yugoslavia, although he is not an expert, as well as two representatives of the OSCE and others. On no bodies did we find any intravital or post-mortem effects of blunt or sharp mechanical weapons or any blunt weapons. After every post-mortem, the findings and report were coordinated with those of the experts from Belorussia and 24 of them with the Finnish experts. That is because they turned up later on. During the overall procedure and the conducting of each post-mortem, a tape was made with the soundtrack as well and two or three cameras were used. The criminal investigation association and the Finnish team of experts all took part." All this is contained in this document and may I -- it please be introduced into evidence. And as I say, the number I read out was the number on the document in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, have you got a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I haven't yet managed to track down which particular document it is. It looks as though it may have come from the Racak binder, which will be helpful and interesting because of course the whole Racak binder will become an exhibit of the Prosecution's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the accuse would like to tell us where it comes from, it would make life a bit easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. It has your number here. K0212750. That is the number. 47 from the beginning, 12747 from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you know about all this, what I've just read out and quoted from that document?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And at the time, did you have the official report by the investigating Judge under the number that it has - I don't want to waste time reading it out - in which it was noted not only the number of weapons that were found on the 15th of January but your threats and demands that procedure be undertaken against the law of criminal proceedings? Are you aware of that note, that report?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which document you're referring to. There are quite a lot that we've dealt with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the official note which speaks about the report made by the investigating Judge, and it is 14/99, the number. And that is where you will find the quotation I read out. I don't want to put it up on the overhead projector, but I consider that it should be admitted into evidence as well, as an exhibit. And now my next question: At the time, you were informed of the minutes on the investigation, on-site investigation, because it was done in the presence of the OSCE, two Americans Gil Giverson [phoen] and L. Sullivan, as well as an Italian who was there by the name of Giovanni Fantini [phoen]. Then there was a forensic expert, Professor Dobricanin [phoen], and an interpreter Atah Damaj [phoen]. And nobody had any objections to make with respect to the investigation and on-site investigation conducted, and the public Prosecutor was there, Ismet Suftu [phoen], who was an Albanian himself. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the incident is that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the minutes on the -- about the on-site investigation. The minutes about the investigation conducted on the spot. And it was done in the presence of these individuals whom I mentioned. And it is -- the minutes were compiled on the 18th of January, 1999, and it says the place of the event was attended by two Americans, Gil Giverson and L. Sullivan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- as well as an Italian, Giovanni Fantini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to read more slowly, but you've read this already. General, can you help us to this? Do you know anything about the minutes of the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of them specifically. They were certainly never brought to my attention by General Loncar, who was the normal means whereby information from the -- from the FRY side would be handed to us. So, no, I'm not aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But if your representatives were present, that is to say these two Americans and one Italian, then I suppose it is their duty to inform you of the minutes that were compiled at an investigation which they attended. So your employees attended, so you must have known. And it says, among other things here, that they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness says he didn't know. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many meetings at which people from the OSCE were present at which the FRY authorities present took minutes. At no stage am I aware of those minutes being made available to us at the time, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in these minutes with your three people plus an interpreter, also one of yours, says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot assist as to the minutes. He knows nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear, then, that the investigation on the spot was attended by three representatives of the OSCE plus a fourth person who was an interpreter, who was a technical person, but three representatives, basically, the ones enumerated here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to tender this into evidence as well, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. No doubt that will be part of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the second document. The first document we have tracked down. It was provided separately and is, I think, not part of the binder. So we're sending for documents of that and we'll have them brought down. And if the Chamber so decides, they will be produced as an exhibit. The second one we'll have to track down in the same way. It takes a minute or so because all it has is a number or some other --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Do I need to get permission from the other side to tender documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's more convenient if they can produce copies. But you can put this document in since it can't be traced. If you want to hand it in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. I am handing them in, all three of them, all three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps you can give them numbers. Just a moment while they're exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document which is numbered K0212747 will be Defence Exhibit Number 2. And the second document, which appears to be KPN.6P.14/99, that will be Defence Exhibit 3 ter, and the third document will be -- appears to be the same document. So there's only two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I handed over three documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The third document will be Defence Exhibit number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you give me a precise yes or no answer: Did you know anything about the contents in these documents, regardless of the fact that you say that the documents are unknown to you as such? But what about the contents, the contents that I quoted? Was that something that you were aware of or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as you stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know at the time about the final report by the Prosecution, which is by law the institution that says whether grounds exist for filing a criminal suit or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we were not there to enforce FRY law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the mission was duty-bound to cooperate with the organs of power and authority on whose territory it was and to inform -- be informed and inform about procedures of any kind, particularly if they were criminal proceedings. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what we did at Racak, and we asked for the people involved to be investigated fully, and that never happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to remind you here that the Prosecution, who is the sole organ, according to Yugoslav law, that is competent to do so, "undertake all steps to refute an armed attack launched by the terrorist organisation called the KLA and in conformity with the law on internal affairs."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may I tender this document into exhibit as well -- into evidence as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As these facts are not something that was of interest to you, in your report of the 15th of January, you report that in Racak, by the verifiers, it was ascertained that one Albanian was killed and that five others were wounded. All this changed in the space of one day, without an investigation, without an expert finding, and everything was ignored. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we reported on the Friday night was what we had seen. What we reported on Saturday was what we had seen. In between Friday night and Saturday night, we saw a lot more. We counted a lot more dead bodies, and we made our own conclusions how they had died. We also invited your representative, General Loncar, to come with us, and he could have been there on Saturday and he could have seen it at the same time as we did. He declined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Don't you know that the fighting with the KLA took place in three villages in the vicinity on that same day?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that your forces fired into several villages in that vicinity, not just Racak. All the way down the valley, the villages were fired into, yes. At no stage did I see any evidence of casualties to the KLA, nor was I ever shown weapons or uniforms which may have been worn or used by these KLA. It is my belief that they ran away very early on in the action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know that Racak was a stronghold of the KLA, in fact?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I certainly didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, for example, that Hashim Thaci, for a BBC interview confirmed that Racak was the KLA stronghold and that there was serious fighting going on there? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be very interested to know when he said that and to whom and in what circumstances. It sounds like being wise after the event to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No I'm talking about his subsequent interview to the BBC. And that is easy to find, it's all public evidence so it can be ascertained. But do you know about it? If you don't, just say no.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Maisonneuve when he returned from Racak on the first day? Did he tell you that in the Racak, from the launching of the operations, the KVM foreign reporters and journalists were present? Did he happen to mention that to you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he knew and I knew, and the reports of the people who were there before him were included in the reports that came to us that night, but they were only able to tell us what they could see from the hillside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you said yourself during the first examination here that your forces went into Racak that day and they didn't stay up on the ridge. Are you changing your testimony now or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you different things that happened at different times. First there were people on the ridge who had arrived after the operation had started and who observed the firing into the village and reported that back to us. Maisonneuve arrived and conferred with them and then he and others went into the village after the firing had stopped at the end of the day after your police were leaving the village. At that point, they talked to the villagers, were told that there were wounded people, one person was dead, and that those were the main things they were concerned about at that moment. That was their main priority, to get the wounded to medical care. That was what they did. At that stage, no one was aware that the people up on the hill had been killed. And I would repeat again: By this stage, it was getting dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You probably knew about the fact that the bodies that you describe had on them several layers of clothing, boots and other clear indices characteristic of people spending a lot of time outside, say, for example, in trenches or the like. Do you remember that, those details?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that several of the dead were wearing wellington boots which are not useful in cold country, so I would say that they were not all -- they were not dressed for fighting in the open and living in the open; they were dressed for working outside as farmers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we don't have a lot of time, it's running out very fast, I ask that the testimony which the other side gave here of Dr. Dusan Dunjic, who describes the state of affairs in which the bodies were found, to be tendered into evidence. So it is a statement, a Prosecution statement, and refers to Dr. Dusan Dunjic. I haven't got the number here, haven't jotted down the number, but I think the name will be sufficient for you to pinpoint the document and I ask that it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that for at least 13 out of the 45 persons who are listed as killed, there are no tombstones, graves at the cemetery in Racak called the Martyrs' Cemetery?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I know that when we counted up the number of dead that had been found in the different locations, it came to either 45 or 46 at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time, during your stay there, do you know that bullets were found which had been shot from different positions, typical of armed combat, in the bodies?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the bullets were found in the bodies, and I know what the state of the bodies was when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However -- now, do you know - and could this have led you to make different assessments - what the foreign press wrote about and reported? I quoted the Berliner Zeitung and Konkret [phoen] and so on and so forth. I quoted those to you. Now I'm going to quote something else, a portion from Elzecer [phoen] book Racak and Mrs. Ranta. It says only the Berliner Zeitung, in the German papers, dealt with this issue. On the 13th of March, 1999, it was published. "High representatives of OSCE were told that 45 Albanians were uncovered in mid-January in the village of Racak and that they were not the victims of Serb massacres over civilians. It says internally in the OSCE that this was rigged by the Albanian side and that the results were achieved from the centre of the Kosovska Mission, that is to say, independently of the expertise" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. Who is this author you're quoting, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Elzecer, and the book is "Racak and the vagaries of Mrs. Ranta." And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt you can call the witness -- the author to give evidence if you want, but it's pointless putting it to this witness. It's simply his or her opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that a statement published on the 17th of March was composed of only five pages and the overall report, according to the Berliner Zeitung was 21 kilogrammes in weight?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please speak -- read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 17th of March, I was getting -- making --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Oskar Fischer [phoen] was the presiding officer of the European organisation at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. On the 17th of March, I was checking the evacuation plans so that we could get everybody out on the 20th if we were ordered to. That was my top priority at that moment. I'm afraid that I was no longer worrying about Racak at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. But do you know that it was noted that the victims were not massacred with their heads cut off and only one case were there traces of a blunt object? In two cases, the heads were post-mortemly cut off. Do you -- by animals, eaten away by animals. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that one of the corpses down in the village had been decapitated. Yes. That is what we saw on the Saturday afternoon. Beyond that, the corpses on the hill, which were the group of, I think, about 23, were the ones which had been shot and had all fallen down all over one another. That was what we saw, that was what we reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know of this assertion by experts who say that if killings are undertaken -- executions are undertaken under command, then the -- the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to read more solely. It is impossible to translate at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are asked to slow down. And in any event, who are you quoting now, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quoting a report by the Pages blanches insérées aux fins d’assurer la correspondance entre la pagination anglaise et la pagination française. Pages 4770 to 4777. forensics -- forensic experts. And in the addendum, it says: "The contradictions between the information received and the results of forensic autopsy can be discarded only if we confirm or refute the cause of death." This refers to the first reports by Walker, who stated that it was the Serbs who had committed the massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not -- it's not a matter for the witness. This is something we are going to have to determine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you're not going to accept this, then, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you allow for the possibility that the bodies had been brought in, transported from somewhere else, et cetera? Do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the impression I gained at the time up on the hill. The bodies were too intermingled and jumbled over one another for that to be a possibility, in my view and in the view of those who were there with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know about what the Times said on the 20th of January, 1999? And he says precisely that the bodies had been brought in, on the basis of what the French journalist said. They come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the opinion of a journalist. It's of no use to us now. We're dealing with evidence. The witness has given his answer to the question which you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's skip the journalist then. But I cannot skip over Helena Ranta, who speaks differently from you in relation to the possibility of having manipulated the bodies. Here's an opportunity to jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the next video clip please be shown, and I kindly ask the interpreters to interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There was doubt here as to whether there was really a massacre in Racak. It pointed out something else and this is the first time she speaks of it for television spectators. "I am aware of the fact that this entire scene had been rigged, because that is indeed possible to do. That is what our first findings had indicated. Also, later forensic examinations that we carried out on the scene in 1999 show that, and we gave the results directly to the International Tribunal in The Hague. "Ambassador Walker came to Racak on Saturday, and that was his very own decision, to qualify the event as a massacre. I have systematically avoided the use of that term. "There is a suspicion that it was a massacre. What could have led to that in Racak? Helena Ranta has information to the effect that among the persons who were dead in Racak were members of the KLA as well. "At that time, Racak was a KLA stronghold. I am convinced that there is quite a bit of information that at that time there were undoubtedly conflicts, clashes between the KLA and the Serb forces. There is no doubt about that. "In addition to that, it was said to me, and I read information about that, that at that place and on that day, members of the KLA were killed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. General, is there anything you can say about that? No doubt we shall hear this -- this witness in due course, but as far as you're concerned, is there anything useful that you can say about her opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, you can call the witness. But the fact that we see something on television isn't evidence of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as for this particular lady witness, the other side have been mentioning her. And we see that the witness precisely speaks of that, that Walker used the word "massacre" and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over this. Now, your time is limited with this witness, so it would be an idea to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I shall continue. However, I would like you to play the next video clip, just one more, and then there's another one after that, but we're going to wait for that next one. Now the following one, please. I hope I haven't made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Walker gathered about 30 journalists, went there with them and, after a short while, he said that this was a massacre committed by the Serbs. "At that moment, he could not have made any kind of judgement. However, this opinion was taken over by the OSCE, the United Nations, all governments of the world. "A day later, NATO met at an extraordinary meeting, which was quite unusual. With this kind of behaviour, Walker had lit the fuse of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to repeat things yet again because Mr. May opposes this. What Christopher Chatelle [phoen] said in Le Monde and also what Le Figaro said - and I quoted these sources earlier - and they say contrary to what you have been saying. However, the question is the following: Since there were many statements made by persons who were there, did such statements encourage you to take a more comprehensive view of this matter, especially because the post-mortem had not been carried out yet, or the investigation? Simply one day Walker's statements, the next day the NATO extraordinary meeting before anything is actually established in relation to such a complex event. What would your explanation of this be?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these journalists weren't on that hillside. The people that were on that hillside with me were unanimous in their view that those people who were dead had been killed by your forces and had not been resisting at the time. We, at the time, asked or called for a joint investigation which might have established more facts, and you could have gone along and agreed with that investigation. You could have suspended the commanding officer while the investigation went on. You did nothing in that matter. Therefore, we ended up drawing our own conclusions. And I have given you my conclusions as I remember them at the time. And I still think that they are as I gave them at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the time is moving on, and we must go out on to another topic. You have put very fully and at length a series of opinions about this matter. The witness has answered as best he could. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is my understanding that I have an entire hour left, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but going over the same point from different directions over and over again is of no assistance to the Court and wastes time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very important point, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree. It is an important point, but you have covered it fully. You have put a series of opinions to the witness which he can't deal with. He's given his evidence. Now, if there's something you want to ask him about what he saw, then you can, but simply putting opinions to him is of no assistance to anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Eamon Smith?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I think there's quite a lot of people with the name Smith around, so I may have missed a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a verifier, an Irish officer, the first one who found the corpses. He stated that there were many casings there, practically only ammunition coming from AK47's. Are you aware of the fact that this ammunition was used by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both sides used the AK47, yes. It was the weapon of choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. The OSCE report on KLA armament says: "The KLA used different kinds of small arms but most often AK47's. The largest number came from Albania after that country, in 1997, sunk into political and economic chaos." Do you know this from OSCE reports?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was observing the events in Albania in 1997 and I know that armouries were ransacked and a lot of weapons went missing, but the AK47 was also used by all of your forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, our forces did not have Chinese manufactured ammunition. Are you aware of that or are you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that the batch numbers were ever made available to us. I'm certainly aware of an ability to use the other side's weapons. It's been done many times in the past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I did not hear that that was ever established in the conflicts in Kosovo and Metohija and that the army and the police took ammunition from the KLA. Is this some new piece of information that you are providing here and now?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am saying simply that I was not aware that only the KLA were using Chinese ammunition, and I saw no evidence to suggest that only the KLA were using Chinese ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exclusively, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on, the question couldn't make clear if the Irishman named Smith has asserted that the ammunition is Chinese. Or if the questioning made clear, the transcript is deficient. I don't have the statement at hand. It might help if we clarified that before losing it by passage of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, we are going to have that clarified some other time because I don't have time right now to go into this particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please answer my following question: Are you aware of the findings of Dr. Milan Stulic, a professor at the University of Belgrade, at the school of law there? After a detailed analysis, he came to the conclusion that all persons killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can put this evidence before us in due course. There's no point, again, putting more opinions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am asking whether the witness is aware of this analysis made by Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well -- are you aware, General, of the analysis of the professor from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When we take all of this into account, is Diana Johnson perhaps right, on the 13th of May, 1999, in Paris, when she says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's more opinions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last time you said that the order "terrorism" is an emotive word and it is more appropriate to use the term "the rebels." However, you stated in a document disclosed by the Prosecution, that is your diagram DZ, Serb version 0304656.60, on the right-hand side, you said, "Terrorism all over the province." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been. What is -- please, what is the point of the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the point is that last time, when I asked you about terrorism, you said that you did not wish to use the word "terrorism" because it's an emotive word, and in your own diagram, you wrote, "terrorism all over the province." In your diagram. So you then used this emotive term, as you had referred to it. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were moments when we did use the word "terrorist" to describe activity, and we did it deliberately to make the point that most of the time we were not using the word. So when there were activities which were genuinely designed, in our view, to terrorise the population, we used the word "terrorist." And so we tried to use it more specifically not as a general catchall phrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a convenient moment for our break. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, you have 50 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware of the Security Council Resolution 1160, dated the 31st of March, 1998? You are aware of its contents, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Resolution 1199 of the 23rd of September, 1998?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also Resolution 1203 of the 24th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all these Resolutions, terrorism in Kosovo is referred to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to check them, but I know that it is referred to in at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned these three to you in which it is mentioned. Do you know and do you believe that the KLA is a terrorist organisation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I think it had some elements which were -- which were capable of terrorist acts. I'm not convinced that the whole thing was a terrorist organisation. At the time, I thought that some of the resistance was as a result of the actions of your forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, do you know about the statement made by Gelbard, the US representative for the Balkans, who was also an expert on terrorism, that he said that the KLA was a terrorist organisation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically know where or when he said that, but if that's his opinion, I -- I acknowledge that that was his opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask that the book be admitted into evidence as well, the book that was brought into these proceedings by the Prosecution. That is a book by Human Rights Watch. It's called "Under Order." It quotes Gelbard's authentic statement in this regard, that is to say with regard to the nature of the KLA as a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to put it in, let's have a look at it. Or you can put it in after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was provided by the other side in its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not waste any further time about it. We'll have the Prosecution look for it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's already exhibited. I'll give you the number in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Since you gave a descriptive answer and in rather relative terms, could you please give me a yes or no answer to the question whether the KLA is a terrorist organisation or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered it as best he can, and he's certainly not going to be badgered for a further answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. This is a general and the executive chief of the Verification Mission in Kosovo. This is his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to get any further on this particular point. We know what you say about it. We will hear some evidence. General, unless there's anything useful you think you might be able to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I can say, sir, that I do think they had terrorist elements in them, but I do not think that every member of this organisation was a terrorist as such. Many of the things that I saw would have made me think about joining the KLA if I had been an Albanian living there at the time. So there were moments when one's sympathy was certainly aroused for the local people because of the outrageous acts committed on them by the forces of law and order who were supposed to be protecting them. I think I've probably gone further than my testimony is supposed to on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, at least for the time when you were in Kosovo, about the crimes that were carried out against both Serbs and Albanians and Turks and Romany, various members of the population, by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware that the police suffered well over a hundred casualties in the year from March 1998 to March 1999, and that was clearly reprehensible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But except for the police, are you aware of all the civilian casualties among the Serb and Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, and I think I referred to the moments when bodies were found early in the morning at various times and generally at a rate of about four a week throughout the period from January through 'til when we left in March 1999. So, yes, we were aware of all of this level of underlying violence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Last time you mentioned on the events that took place in the village of Rogovo. In the document that the Prosecution provided together with your statement, with the diagram DZ, and the number was 03045366, and it was under point 85, in fact, where you spoke about Rogovo, and I quote: "Probably a shelter of the KLA but not all of them were armed," words to that effect. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's more or less what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And last time, you also commented when photographs were shown of members of the police force, you commented that they were not typically dressed and accorded special weight to the circumstances and emphasised the police force, the police, as being the perpetrators of some kind of alleged crime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I had some doubts as to the circumstances in which the action took place. Specifically, I was very surprised that in an action such as took place, no one was captured alive and no one was wounded, which seemed very odd if you look at any normal exchange of fire when at least as many people get wounded as get killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, precisely because of a statement of yours like that, I should like to ask the technical booth to play the next excerpt, which relates to that, in fact. And it's the last remaining excerpt that I shall be playing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we hear the soundtrack as well, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "29th of January 1999, 24 Albanians were killed and one Serb policeman. So there was a clash. It was not a massacre of civilians, as the Defence Minister claimed. "The historians and a foreign television crew provide evidence of what actually happened. Arms next to Albanians who were allegedly civilians. But they're wearing uniforms, and some of them had KLA insignia. "The first observer of the OSCE that came to the spot was this man on the left here. He is German policeman Henning Hensch [phoen]. It is true what the Defence Minister said on the first day in his statement that I saw via Deutsche Welle, but this does not coincide with what I saw. Nevertheless, the official report about the event in Rogovo speaks about a massacre over civilians -- of civilians. We found a minivan there with 14 bodies that had been bullet-ridden. Three bodies were outside the vehicle. In the garage, there were five more bodies of KLA fighters wearing uniforms. "Three hundred metres away, we found four more bodies. The bodies that the Defence Minister showed, we collected together and placed them in one spot. The Serb policemen, myself, and my two Russian colleagues. "So that's how this filming came into being about the alleged execution as Minister Sharpe presented itself and they have nothing to do with what actually happened. It was quite clear that this was no case of massacre of the civilian population because, according to the OSCE, even the KLA commanders said that it was the fighters that had lost their lives there, fighting for the cause and ideal of Greater Albania. And the German minister, apart from that, turned it into a massacre."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw there what the German policeman said, who was a member of your mission and who claims that it is true that what his minister stated does not correspond to what he saw on the spot and that it does not correspond with his report, the report that he sent in. Now, did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't know about what the German minister said, but I can remind you of what I said I saw, which was that, I think, four people were wearing KLA uniforms, and I think 12 weapons were shown as having been found with the KLA, or with the civilians, four of whom were in KLA uniform. And I think I said that at the time in front of cameras as well, with General Loncar there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. Explain this to me as a soldier. If the police are shot at from 12 rifles and not 25, can the police count the rifles that the shooting was done from and then establish whether it would return fire or not, and are the 12 rifles that they were shot at, is that too little, even if there were only 12, as you yourself claim? Would that be considered too little, too few?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what happened at the scene when the police attacked, but I found it remarkable that everybody was killed who appeared to be on the -- inside that compound who was male. I don't know how many weapons were actually in the hands of the people inside. They could have been brought into the scene from outside by anybody, because there was a quite a long lapse between the incident and my people being allowed in to look at it, and your people were inside there throughout all of that time when mine had no access. So those 12 weapons could have been planted. Had there been good forensic evidence, had there been a proper forensic inquiry, then these facts could have been established. But you can't establish the facts when the investigating Judge comes in, spends one hour sloshing around in the ankle-deep mud and declares the investigation over, which is what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you say that all of them were killed, do you allow for the fact that someone might have escaped?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some might have escaped, but I'm surprised, of the 25 killed, there were no wounded. That would make me worried as to what happened at the end of the fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. A moment ago when you were describing everything that could have happened, theoretically speaking, that anything could have happened, now, on the basis of those assumptions that something could have happened but perhaps did not happen, would that be sufficient to interpret -- give an interpretation of the event which would give rise to a reaction, the kind of reaction that condemns, although it was obvious that it was a clash between the KLA and the police forces?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the fact that it was a clash between the KLA and the police forces does not give the police forces of any nation carte blanche to go in and kill everybody. Why were they not apprehended and put on trial?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you maintain that an execution was carried out or that -- whether those men died in battle? All reports say that those people were killed in battle.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the reports I've seen said that they were dead when we arrived. I don't know what happened at the end of the action. It is possible that people, all of them, were killed in battle, 25 of them sharing 12 weapons. It doesn't fit my experience of the KLA. They tended not to fight when they were confronted with overwhelming force; they tended to run away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps something like that did happen to a part of that group, namely that they did escape.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I'm surprised that we haven't met some of this large number of people that might have escaped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you, nevertheless, say perhaps -- you say perhaps - a conditional sentence - that perhaps it might have been a clash between the KLA and MUP. You use the conditional tense.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because this was two weeks after Racak, so it was in everyone's interest that any significant event like this was properly investigated and the facts established beyond reasonable doubt, and there seemed very little appetite among your people on the ground to do that. That was what made me suspicious, but no more than that because I had no evidence, otherwise I would have stated it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But at that time you made no comment or objection to the cooperation between the police and the Verification Mission. You made no criticism of it.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not seeking more antagonism between the police and the verification unit at the time. I certainly did not express any satisfaction with what had been done. I described with General Loncar, in front of cameras, what I had been shown and made the point at the time of the time that had elapsed between arriving and being shown what was inside the compound. So you're right, I didn't speculate. I didn't think at that stage it was helpful to. The situation there was quite critical as a result of Racak, as a result of Walker having been made persona non grata. There was a lot of media speculation. I was not prepared to add to it in a way that would have been unhelpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm sure you know that on that particular day, the 29th of January, 1999, at about 6.30 a.m., in that village of Rogovo, the Gjakove municipality, at a municipal patrol of the Djakovica SUP, a terrorist attack was launched by a rather large group of KLA members where Rakovic Predrag, a policeman was killed. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that's correct. That's the account we were given but we didn't have people there at the time. I know a policeman was killed. I know that, in general, there was a clash between MUP and KLA in the early hours of that morning at that place. I do not know what specifically happened, what the sequence of events was, who started -- who started what, who saw each other first, who fired first, whether anybody attempted to surrender, what subsequently happened. I just don't know any of that, and that is why a proper forensic examination at the time would have been in everybody's interest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why, then, did you not ask for an examination of that kind if you had your doubts at the time?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually did. We attempted to get the Finnish forensic team to stay on and carry out that investigation, but that was not possible for reasons that I wasn't -- that were never made clear to me. I certainly said let's do a proper forensic examination, and I certainly commented on the fact that it's very difficult to ascertain what precisely happened in an area several hundred metres square that is a very, very slushy, dirty, muddy area inside an hour. I felt it was a most inadequate investigation at the time and said so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that then, after the killing of the policeman -- or, rather, the attack by a large group of terrorists on the patrol, police patrol of the SUP of Djakovica, that the group of terrorists fled to the house of Seladin Salaja from whence it opened fire on the members of the police force and that, after that, they found the rifle belonging to the policeman who was killed, in the house, Predrag Rakovic?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my reading of what happened. As I recall it, one of the corpses was found having been shot sitting on the lavatory. You don't go to the lavatory if you're in the middle of an exchange of fire. So there were suspicious circumstances about this -- this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you informed of the fact that the house of Berisha Xhderit was a terrorist base in Rogovo? Precisely in yard of that house was where the terrorists were killed.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We later were informed, I believe, that that was used as a terrorist safe house, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that from the van, the Isuzu van - I don't want to quote the licence plates - which was in the courtyard of this particular house, that they shot at the policeman from there, just as they did from the house? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But there were over 200 bullet holes in that red van, and I think most of them were made by bullets going into it, not coming out of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I assume that you as a soldier know full well that when you shoot out of a van, you can't find holes from the bullets exiting from the -- fired from the weapons that were used to shoot at the policemen. Is that logical or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my point is I have no idea precisely what went on in the courtyard, but I know what I saw when I went into the courtyard, and the people -- and the van had been riddled with fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it logical that if the shooting -- isn't that logical if the shooting was coming from the van, if they were shooting at the policemen from the van?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- you don't shoot through the body of the van in order to shoot out of the van, no. I would say if you are going to shoot from inside the van, you shoot through the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your country, when criminals shoot at the police, it is allowed only to shoot through the windows and not at a vehicle? It has to hit the window -- the windows; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the police shoot at criminals, they shoot aimed shots and they account for every round they fire. There is no evidence that that ever happened with your police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that this group was led with the infamous Yahi Ibrahimaj [phoen] who was the organiser of the attack on the members of the police force two days previously, that is to say on the 27th of January, 1999, at the Bishtrizhine place when two policemen were seriously wounded? Do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there had been an attack on the police, and if you'd been able to catch the perpetrator on put him on trial, you could have sent him to gaol for a long time. But you would have needed evidence that stood up in court to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So despite all these assumptions, the ones that you've been talking about, and last time you saw a photograph of the van and the police forces, the bodies of the terrorists, and you come to a conclusion that it was in fact their liquidation. Is that a correct description, would you say, of what you did?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never said it was their liquidation in so many words, but I have always expressed doubt that so many people could be killed in such a way without anyone attempting to surrender and being -- being taken prisoner. Furthermore, the lack of evidence that was ever produced, the lack of a proper investigation at the time all makes me worry, in the context of where we were and when we were at the time, with Racak two weeks behind us, with the Contact Group meeting the next day, that it was in everybody's interest that the facts of this event be made as clear as possible. And I never detected any willingness on any of your officials to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Do you know that 14 automatic rifles made in China, not 12, as you said, but 14 made in China were found and a large quantity of ammunition as well, a pistol, the Zbrojovka, and six made-in-China bombs, grenades, a bulletproof vest, US-produced, and that in Xhderit Berisha's yard some spoons were found and bombs which were also made in China. Do you know -- are you aware of this whole list of things, of items that was discovered on the basis of the investigation carried out on the spot, on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of weapons I counted was 12. I did not see -- I think I may have seen a bulletproof vest but I wasn't aware that possession of a bulletproof vest was a capital offence anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about that. All I'm doing is reading out a list of items found. I don't want to skip over a single of those items which might comprise fighting and combat equipment, and civilians don't usually wear bulletproof vests, especially the parts of the bombs that were found testified to the fact that not only did the shooting come from the house and the van but that grenades were thrown at the police as well. Does that seem to you be something that would be logical or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no reports of grenades being thrown at any time. I only heard reports of small-arms fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So grenades are heavy weaponry; is that it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the fire that was described by the people who described it to me and to my people was of small-arms fire, that is, rifles and automatic weapons. I don't recall hearing about grenades being used. But I'm not really sure what the relevance of whether they were or were not used was because both sides had access to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, these were parts of bombs and grenades that were made in China. I quoted that a moment ago from the report, the on-site report. So they weren't thrown by members of the police force. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it would have been terrific to have captured some of these people alive, to have put them on trial, to have produced all this evidence, and as I said, to have sentenced them in a proper court of law to a prison sentence. That's what everybody else does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Now, do you know how many terrorists were taken into custody in Kosovo and brought before a court of law?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were quite a lot of people who were detained, and we expended quite a lot of effort as a mission attempting to gain access to the prisons so that these people could be -- could be talked to. I'm not aware of very much access having been accorded, but I was not the member of the mission whose task this was. I am, however, aware that these requests were made and were routinely denied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about something else, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. If you are suggesting that the police force did not wish to arrest these people but wished to kill them, then how come so many terrorists were indeed detained, taken into custody, and taken to court if it was indeed the police's intention to kill them rather than take them into custody? Why did it not then kill all those that it had arrested and taken to court?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my experience that every time there was an attack on armed -- armed KLA, that there were very few prisoners ever taken. In my experience, I was aware of three incidents in which over a hundred people were killed and only -- only nine were taken prisoner. That's -- and I know that at the first of those incidents, on the border in December, a lot ran away. But nonetheless, the lack of prisoners in these exchanges does seem very odd to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, in this connection, in regard of this incident which you mentioned and brought up once again, in your first testimony you expressly stated that it was a legal ambush at the border. Do you still maintain that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think it was a legal act for a sovereign state to defend its borders against people carrying weapons in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to Rogovo. Do you know that two terrorists wore camouflage uniforms, four black uniforms with KLA insignia, while the rest wore different kinds of semi-military clothing and that they were identified? I don't want to spend my time by reading all of these names, but a large number of them among those who were identified are not from the village of Rogovo. That is to say, they come from Klecka, Donji Ratis, Smolnice, Jablanica, Bucani, Drenje, Svarahiren [phoen], et cetera. Doesn't that seem unusual to you that a large number of those persons who lost their lives were not from the village of Rogovo? Therefore, they were a formation that was not attached to that particular locality.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite prepared to accept that they didn't live in Rogovo, that they may well have been moving from somewhere, probably in Albania, to somewhere further east within Kosovo and that they overnighted in Rogovo, yes, okay, but that doesn't mean they all had to be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get this idea that the police had the intention of killing all of them? They were simply exposed to fire from 6.30 a.m. And I said that to you awhile ago. It's not that the police attacked them, they attacked the police patrol, and then they fled and then they continued to shoot at the police.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one possible interpretation of the events, but I have no personal knowledge that that was the case. I have said what I saw. There were 25 dead people. Four of them were in KLA uniform. I saw 12 weapons. It is quite possible that they had all been using the house as a safe house overnight and were proposing to move on elsewhere into Kosovo the next day. They may well all have been KLA members. But I still don't see why they all had to be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you find it possible that what the police report says is true, that is to say that they killed a policeman first and that then these men got killed during the crossfire with the police? Do you allow for that possibility or do you preclude it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's certainly possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that in the monthly report of the OSCE from the 20th of February 1999 that pertains to the period between mid-January and mid-February, it says that one of the commanders of the KLA in Pec admitted that 18 out of 25 terrorists were members of the KLA as far as this event was concerned? Are you aware of that? That's what it says in your report.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that coming in. We got that information certainly several days, if not weeks, after the event. It was not at odds with our view of the event, that it may well have been a safe house used by the KLA because people were coming in from Albania on their way into the rest of Kosovo. So that was not different to what we saw as a possible scenario.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You established in the document that the Prosecutor attached to your statement, that's the diagram DZ 03044567, under number 120, that you are concerned that the KLA leadership is losing control over KLA zones. My question is: Why were you concerned?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was clear to us that the KLA were, from time to time, not obeying the orders that they received down their chain of command. It always took a long time for their orders to get down the chain of command. But there were moments when we felt that they were -- they were not restraining themselves at a time when their high command had told them to restrain themselves. I think it was specifically when Rambouillet was on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last time, you provided a table containing violations of Security Council resolutions. Bearing in mind your system of designation, it seems that it was only the army of Yugoslavia that was violating the Resolution. However, if you look at the contents, many violations came from the KLA. For example, on page 20, the incident from the 22nd and 25th of January. You said this was a violation. This empty space means it was the fault of the army of Yugoslavia. And in the description of the 22nd, you say: "In Nebola the KLA abducted five Serb civilians. They say that they will not release them until the FRY releases nine Albanians from a border incident. The KLA threatens to start a new war at 0800 hours," et cetera, et cetera. How can you call that a violation by the army? Or this other example that I mentioned of the 25th of January. Again, the space is filled out the same way. You say: "In Glogovac, the Verification Mission heard firing and the MUP said that they had wounded a member of the KLA who was shooting at -- who was shooting at him. The authorities showed an AK47 with ammunition belts which allegedly belonged to the wounded person, who was arrested and taken to hospital in Pristina." How can that be an incident that you ascribe to the forces of Yugoslavia? Both of them, actually. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to go through that -- through that entire table. The table was designed to show the sort of events that were happening and to show the level of violence that was happening on both sides. I think that was established quite specifically by that document. However, I was not the author of that document. That was put together by -- by some of the researchers in Pristina, and it was sent to, I think, the Security Council to indicate the level of compliance by both sides with their Security Council Resolutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But this was under your control. So irrespective of whether -- well, look at the 20th of January, for instance. Again a violation of the Security Council Resolution. You give the following description: "Three brothers were arrested for having weapons." That is to say, illegal possession of a weapon. What is the incident involved that is ascribed to the forces of Yugoslavia? On the 20th of January, you say - page 19 of this document of yours - you say: "The village was surrounded by members of the MUP with eight to ten vehicles. Three brothers, two teachers, and a doctor were arrested for possession of weapons." That is to say, nobody was killed. The police was conducting a search. You know that according to the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, illegal possession of weapons entails the possibility of a rather high prison sentence. I don't have to go into all of that now. So what is the violation committed by the Yugoslavs? Then you have here those empty spaces of yours, the little blanks that mean that it was the Yugoslav authorities that violated the Security Council Resolution. Also on the 20th of January, you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About time we had a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About time we had a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And also, even if the general can follow what the accused is asking him, there's nothing on the ELMO to assist the rest of the public to follow what is being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Time is going on. Mr. Milosevic, you have got three more minutes. Is there a question you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, but of course I have many more questions. Unfortunately, then I have to leave this diagram. It was not my understanding that I had only three minutes left. You told me that I had 50 minutes left when we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was 47 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were there any foreign fighters in Kosovo on the KLA side while you were there with the mission?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met any personally. I certainly heard an unconfirmed report that there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your knowledge. I'm not asking you about your encounters. You were the operations chief of the mission. I'm asking you whether you had any knowledge of this, not whether you encountered such persons.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard an unconfirmed report, and I then attempted to find out more about it and was never able to find out anything more about it. So it was not -- it never became fact, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
